purpose: This medicine is used to treat serious bacterial infections, including complicated urinary tract infections, abdominal infections, and certain hospital-acquired pneumonias. It is especially helpful for infections caused by bacteria that are resistant to many other antibiotics. Doctors typically use this when other antibiotic options have not worked or are not expected to work.
how_it_works: Ceftazidime is an antibiotic that works by attacking and breaking down the outer wall of bacteria, which kills them. However, some tough bacteria produce substances called beta-lactamases that can destroy ceftazidime before it gets a chance to work. That is where avibactam comes in — it blocks those bacterial defenses, allowing ceftazidime to do its job and kill the infection.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, constipation, rash, dizziness, and anxiety are among the more common side effects. Some patients may notice changes in kidney lab values. Let your healthcare team know if anything feels unusual or bothersome.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, as the dose may need to be adjusted. A serious and potentially life-threatening type of diarrhea caused by a bacteria called C. difficile can occur — call your doctor right away if you develop severe or watery diarrhea. Allergic reactions, including severe ones, are possible especially if you have had reactions to penicillin or cephalosporin antibiotics before. Neurological effects like seizures have been rarely reported, especially in patients with kidney issues.
typical_dosing: This medication is given through an IV (directly into a vein) in a hospital or infusion center setting — it is not a pill taken at home. The usual adult dose is 2.5 grams given every 8 hours, infused over 2 hours. Treatment usually lasts 5 to 14 days depending on the type and severity of the infection. Your doctor will adjust the dose if you have kidney problems.
